chunks.text: The structure of material in Earth's interior has been probed in considerable detail by measuring the transmission of seismic waves through Earth.
By monitoring the seismic waves in different locations, scientists can learn about the layers through which the waves have traveled.
Oceanic crust covers 55% of Earth's surface and lies mostly submerged under the oceans. It is typically about 6 kilometers thick.
The continental crust is 20 to 70 kilometers thick and is composed predominantly of a different volcanic class of silicates.
The largest part of the solid Earth, called the mantle, stretches from the base of the crust downward to a depth of 2900 kilometers.
The density in the mantle increases downward from about 3.5 g/cm³ to more than 5 g/cm³ as a result of the compression produced by the weight of overlying material.
Beginning at a depth of 2900 kilometers, we encounter the dense metallic core of Earth. With a diameter of 7000 kilometers, our core is substantially larger than the entire planet Mercury.
The outer core is liquid, but the innermost part of the core (about 2400 kilometers in diameter) is probably solid.
